newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq and U.N. argue over arms inspection rights.
newsitem.headline: Iraq and U.N. argue over arms inspection rights.

text.p: Iraq blamed a U.N. Security Council warning for obstructing arms inspectors on a "U.S. fabrication" on Sunday as a senior U.N. arms official met an adviser to President Saddam Hussein over the confrontation.

U.N. spokeswoman Jo Lomas said Charles Deulfer, deputy chairman of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) overseeing elimination of Iraq's prohibited weapons, "discussed recent sensitivities between UNSCOM and Iraq" with Presidential Adviser Amir al-Sa'di.
"They had a long non-confrontational meeting," Lomas told Reuters.

The head of UNSCOM, Rolf Ekeus, had told the U.N. Security Council that Baghdad prevented U.N. inspectors from entering sites and endangered U.N. helicopters and their crews assisting U.N. ground teams.
Late on Saturday, the United Nations Security Council responded by unanimously warning Iraq it faced further sanctions if it obstructed U.N. inspectors.
Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz on Sunday described the resolution as "the outcome of an American fabrication in which Rolf Ekeus took part."
"America feels very nervous because the political isolation which it wanted to impose on Iraq has started to break up," Aziz said in a statement to the Iraqi News Agency INA in New York.
"The allegation that Iraq does not cooperate with the (U.N. Special) Commission is false."
Iraq's U.N. ambassador Nizar Hamdoon described the resolution as "less poisonous than the original U.S. draft resolution but it is still poisonous," INA said in a dispatch from New York.
Duelfer said on his arrival on Baghdad on Saturday that Iraq was still concealing weapons of mass dustruction.
A statement by the Iraqi information ministry carried by INA said Duelfer's "allegations...are groundless," adding he had "committed a great mistake" when he said so.

UNSCOM must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on its oil exports. The U.N. has allowed Baghdad since December to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy urgently needed goods.
The sanctions were imposed following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya said Iraq's former culture and information minister Abdul-al-Ghani Abdul-al-Ghafur urged the United Nations Security Council to put Ekeus on trial because inspectors examined religious sites in Baghdad last week for hidden weapons.
Iraq said on Wednesday an UNSCOM arms team inspected a church and two convents on the outskirts of Baghdad.
